label: Projective Geometry
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 229 to 262 and makes one move visible: discard metric structure, keep only incidence and cross-ratio. Points and lines become homogeneous triples, every two lines meet, and duality lets each theorem be read twice. We then recover affine and Euclidean geometry by choosing extra projective data.

label: Axioms and Points at Infinity
notes: Replacing parallelism with incidence closes every line. Two distinct points determine one line; two distinct lines determine one point, with no exceptions. The affine model explains the familiar case: adjoin one line at infinity, and each family of parallel lines meets at its own point there. The finite plane PG(2,3) audits these axioms with exact counts.

label: Homogeneous Coordinates: Join and Meet
notes: Incidence becomes algebra. A point is a nonzero vector up to scale; a line is a nonzero covector up to scale; incidence is a vanishing dot product. The line joining two points is their cross product, and the point where two lines meet is also a cross product. This single symmetry between points and covectors already encodes duality.

label: The Principle of Duality
notes: Because points and lines enter the axioms symmetrically, every theorem has a dual obtained by swapping point with line, join with meet, collinear with concurrent. Desargues is self-dual; Pascal and Brianchon are duals. Duality halves the work: prove one statement and its mirror is automatically a theorem in the projective plane.

label: Desargues' Theorem
notes: Desargues is the first bridge from configuration to invariant. If corresponding vertices of two triangles lie on three lines through a common centre, the triangles are perspective from a point; then the three intersections of corresponding sides are collinear, lying on the axis of perspective. The notebook builds the configuration and verifies the axis by a single determinant.

label: Pappus' Theorem
notes: Pappus takes two lines, three points on each, and crosses the connecting segments. The three crossing points are collinear. Pappus is the special projective fact that forces the coordinate field to be commutative, so it sits beneath the algebra of homogeneous coordinates. The notebook checks a sample configuration inside the finite plane PG(2,3).

label: The Cross-Ratio
notes: The cross-ratio of four collinear points is the fundamental projective invariant. It is defined from ratios of ratios and is unchanged by any projectivity, even though individual distances are not. Projecting the four points from a centre onto another line preserves the value, so cross-ratio also belongs to the pencil of four concurrent lines, not merely to the marks.

label: Harmonic Conjugates and the Quadrangle
notes: A complete quadrangle has four vertices and six sides meeting in three diagonal points. A line cutting the figure produces a harmonic set: cross-ratio exactly minus one. This is the projective replacement for a metric midpoint relation. Because it is built only from joins and meets, the harmonic conjugate survives every projectivity while lengths do not.

label: Projectivities and Perspectivities
notes: A perspectivity projects one range onto another from a centre; a projectivity is a finite chain of perspectivities. On a coordinate line a projectivity is a fractional linear map. The defining property is that it preserves cross-ratio, and conversely any cross-ratio-preserving correspondence of ranges is a projectivity. The symbolic check confirms invariance for a general nonsingular map.

label: Conics by Steiner's Construction
notes: Steiner defines a conic projectively, without distance. Take two pencils of lines related by a projectivity that is not a perspectivity; the meets of corresponding lines trace a conic. Equivalently a conic is the self-conjugate locus of a polarity: with symmetric matrix Q the polar of point x is the line Qx, and points satisfying x transpose Q x equal zero form the curve.

label: Pascal's Theorem
notes: Pascal is the decisive incidence test for conics. Inscribe a hexagon in a conic; the three pairs of opposite sides meet in three points, and those three points are collinear on the Pascal line. The notebook builds a single conic, forms one hexagon, and confirms the collinearity with one determinant rather than three separate metric curves.

label: Brianchon: The Dual
notes: Dualizing Pascal swaps inscribed for circumscribed and collinear for concurrent. Brianchon's theorem states that for a hexagon whose six sides touch a conic, the three diagonals joining opposite vertices pass through one point. Pascal and Brianchon are a single projective fact seen from the point side and from the line side, the cleanest illustration of duality at work.

label: From Projective Back to Euclidean
notes: Projective space becomes affine when one plane is singled out as the plane at infinity, and Euclidean when that plane also carries an absolute polarity. Directions live where the last coordinate vanishes, and two directions are orthogonal when the absolute polarity pairs them. The ladder of invariants tells incidence from affine from metric before any transformation is applied.
